Q: Reading from Postgres DB using Polars and filter on list of strings A:

Cleanest fix for Postgres is use ANY(%s) instead of IN, Postgres lets you pass an array as one parameter:

mylist = ['abc', '123']

pl.read_database(
    query='SELECT * FROM schema.table WHERE mycol = ANY(%s)',
    execute_options={'parameters': [mylist]},
    connection=con
)

Note parameters: [mylist] is wrapped in a list since the whole list is one bound parameter. Also %s is psycopg2's placeholder style, not ? that's likely why your original wasn't working.

Q: Time limit exceeded in Strings Rotations of Each Other A:

indexOf searches starting from the start of the String, whilst lastIndexOf starts the search from the end. See here and here. So, if s2.equals(s1.substring(n) + s.substring(0, n)), then, if n is 1, that would mean that indexOf first needs to pass n - 1 characters until it gets to the first character of the match and then process n further characters, totalling n - 1 + n = 2n - 1 characters and in this case lastIndexOf would pass 1 character at the end until it reaches the last character of the match and the continuing n further characters, totalling n + 1 character and since 2n - 1 < n + 1 if we presume n to be a large positive, it could have yielded the difference in performance that resulted being the straw that broke the camel's back.

But this difference is casual, not a relevant algorithmic difference, because n could be s2.length() - 1 in which case indexOf would be the quicker one.

Hence, there is no known performance hits in using lastIndex vs. lastIndexOf in general, but actual measures may be different if the test cases so suggest. So, instead of trying to find the esoteric difference, it makes more sense to try and see why your algorithm is not quick-enough so it depends on the test cases. For example

if(s1.equals(s2))   return true;

checks whether two, potentially huge strings are equal and it is time-consuming. Maybe it's worth checking whether the first character matches before doing the big check, like

if((s1.charAt(0) == s2.charAt(0)) && s1.equals(s2))   return true;

Q: how to print the error in a let-else statement in rust? A:

Another option not using let-else is map_err:

let result = function_call_that_returns_a_result().map_err(|e| format!("error: {e}"))?;

Using the ? operator on a mapped error can help keep things clean when your function returns a Result. Mapping the error is great for avoiding the usual ? problem of not being able to attach additional information to errors from other functions.

You can also use inspect_err to perform non-transforming operations e.g. println! in your error handler instead of returning an Into-able for your error type - especially if you don't return an error type! For example, if your function returns an Option, you can use:

let result = function_call_that_returns_a_result().inspect_err(|e| eprintln!("error: {e}")).ok()?

to quickly log the error before converting to Option with ok and returning None in the error case.

Result and Option also have or_else and unwrap_or_else for similar behaviour.

Q: How to download video with JavaScript A:

One important limitation is that not every video can be downloaded simply by finding the <video> or <iframe> URL. Many modern sites use HLS/DASH streams, blob URLs, authentication, or cross-origin restrictions. For a Chrome extension, it may be better to detect the actual media requests (where permitted) and then handle the download through the extension APIs. This is something I’m currently learning while building my first video-downloader extension.

Q: How to handle data which seems like a duplicate but actually is not A:

To decide if something is a duplicate or not, decide what your primary key actually is.

Your table seems to be about orders. Customer name is not sufficient as a primary key for that. What makes an order unique in your data? Do you have an OrderID? Can one person order the same item multiple times? Why are there even duplicates in the data? If you know where they come from, it may be easier to remove them in a correct way. customer_id, datetime is probably an acceptable ad-hoc primary key for analyzising such data, but there is no way to tell without knowing your data and your goals.
